extracted.intended_audience: authors preparing query letters to literary agents (fiction and nonfiction)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for crafting query letters to literary agents, covering openings, length, personalization, bios/platform, disclosures, and tone for both fiction and nonfiction submissions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Query letter purpose
rubrics_metrics.description: At its core, a query letter is a sales document, and so it’s meant to sell. Not explain, not argue, not defend, not plead.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat the query as a sales pitch: focus on selling the work rather than explaining your intent or pleading for representation. Agents know why they're receiving queries; you do not need to state that you’re seeking representation or explain purpose up front.

rubrics_metrics.name: Personalization of the query letter
rubrics_metrics.description: Personalize only if you have something meaningful or specific to say; throwaway lines aren’t going to impress the agent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid floppy, unmemorable personalization such as generic statements ('I’m reaching out because your website says you represent romance'). Only include personalization that is specific and substantive; throwaway lines blend into the background and have little effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Query letter opening
rubrics_metrics.description: Options include a catchy one-sentence hook/log line, a facts-first opening (e.g., 'I’m seeking representation for MY GREAT NOVEL...'), or diving straight into the story premise.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For fiction, generally begin with the story premise—launch into the premise without prefacing that you’re seeking representation or naming the genre. For nonfiction, follow separate nonfiction-structure guidance. If you are a previously published or otherwise credentialed author, starting with a bit about yourself can be appropriate. If you have an exceptional one-sentence pitch, you may start with it, but don’t force a contrived logline.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appropriate query letter length
rubrics_metrics.description: Traditional one-page single-spaced queries are long; for fiction aim for 200–350 words (about half a page single-spaced).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Brevity is your friend. Shorter queries reduce the chance of losing an agent's attention and encourage them to request pages. 150 words can work but often is too short for epic-style novels that require worldbuilding. Avoid book-report summaries that recount plot twists or introduce too many characters.

rubrics_metrics.name: Your bio in the query letter
rubrics_metrics.description: For nonfiction, a bio statement is a near-requirement; for fiction it’s acceptable to omit the bio if you have nothing relevant to say.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include author background when it demonstrates platform or directly informs the work (e.g., an insider writing about their profession). Avoid awkward, irrelevant, or self-discrediting biographical details. Agents rarely reject solely for lack of a bio if the story itself is strong.

rubrics_metrics.name: Information on author platform, marketing, or audience
rubrics_metrics.description: Platform and marketing information are important for nonfiction pitches; novelists usually shouldn’t bother with platform/audience statements unless they have exceptional reach.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Read agent submission guidelines carefully—most will ask for platform for nonfiction but not for novels. If guidelines request only a query letter, keep to genre/category clarity and basic background rather than a full marketing plan. If an agent asks for marketing/platform materials for a novel, that may be a red flag and you could consider querying elsewhere. If you are a social-media celebrity or have a demonstrable large audience, lead with that.

rubrics_metrics.name: Professional editing disclosure
rubrics_metrics.description: Don’t say your manuscript has been professionally edited; the statement has become so common as to be meaningless.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Claiming professional editing rarely improves your chances and can sometimes imply the manuscript needed help; freelance editors vary in quality and can do harm as well as good. Omit this claim from the query.

rubrics_metrics.name: Including praise or endorsements in the query
rubrics_metrics.description: Quoting praise or positive reviews from mentors, editors, critics, or published authors is not helpful unless the person is well known and trusted by the agent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Endorsements from unknowns are unlikely to sway an agent and may raise the question why that person didn’t introduce you. Use endorsements sparingly and only when they carry weight with the recipient.

rubrics_metrics.name: Simultaneous submissions policy and disclosure
rubrics_metrics.description: You don’t have to state that you’re simultaneously cold querying many agents; it’s assumed. But disclose when requested partials or full manuscripts are also under consideration.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not clutter the initial query with statements about wide simultaneous querying. When an agent requests pages, be transparent if other agents are also considering the work and include timelines/deadlines as appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Voice, confidence, and tasteful charm
rubrics_metrics.description: A writer’s voice and sense of confidence matter; queries should have some life but not so much that they distract from the goal of getting an agent to request the manuscript.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: It’s possible to break rules successfully if the result is genuinely charming and distinctive, but know the difference between charming and annoying. Keep personality in the query in balance with clarity and the primary mission of prompting a request to read more.
